opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the start of 2025 I was pretty skeptical. I'm a theoretical physicist working on black holes, specifically the structure of the photon ring and how light orbits near the event horizon, and that's a fairly narrow corner of physics. My sense was that these models were great at writing emails or summarizing papers, but that when you got down to the actual technical work, the long calculations, the subtle approximations, the things only a handful of people in the world think about, they'd fall apart.

I'd tried earlier versions, and the experience was a bit like talking to a very confident undergraduate. They'd produce something that looked right, with all the right words and equations, but if you checked carefully there'd be a sign error, a made-up reference, or a step that didn't follow. In research that's worse than useless, because you spend more time verifying than you'd have spent doing it yourself.

So my working assumption was that this was interesting technology but not really relevant to what I do day to day. Maybe useful for coding a plot or cleaning up LaTeX, not for the physics.

What changed my mind was actually testing it on problems I knew the answers to, things my collaborators and I had worked out over months. I gave it a hard problem, one about the symmetries of certain black hole equations, expecting it to stumble. And it found the answer. It took a while to reason through it, but it got there, and the reasoning held up when I checked it. That was a genuinely startling moment for me. I remember thinking, okay, the ground has shifted, and I need to take this seriously as a tool for real science, not just a curiosity.

r001.rationale: The response says he was skeptical and thought ChatGPT was not relevant to his day-to-day physics work, but it does not say he expected it would take a long time before becoming meaningfully relevant.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the start of 2025 I was pretty skeptical. I work on black holes, on the photon ring, on these very specific questions in general relativity where the math is intricate and the literature is small. I'd tried earlier models and they were fine for writing an email or summarizing something, but when I pushed them on actual physics, they'd confidently make things up. They'd produce an equation that looked plausible and was simply wrong. And in my field, a wrong sign or a wrong factor isn't a small thing, it's the whole result.

So my attitude was basically: this is a nice tool for the mundane parts of the job, maybe for cleaning up prose or helping with code, but it's not going to touch the real work. The real work is the part where you sit with a problem for weeks and slowly figure out what the right question even is.

What changed my mind was actually sitting down and testing it seriously rather than casually. I started giving it the kind of calculations I'd give a strong graduate student, things where I already knew the answer, so I could check. And it was not perfect, but it was much better than I expected. It could follow a derivation, catch when I'd set something up wrong, suggest an approach I hadn't considered. The reasoning models in particular felt different. There was something closer to actual thinking happening, as opposed to pattern matching on text.

I wouldn't say it replaced anything I do. But I went from "this is irrelevant to my science" to "this is a collaborator I should be talking to," and that shift happened faster than I would have predicted.

r001.rationale: The response says Alex initially thought ChatGPT would not touch the real work and that his change of mind happened faster than predicted, but it does not clearly state that he expected meaningful relevance to take a long time.
